Townsend's vole (Microtus townsendii) is a small arvicoline rodent inhabiting the coastal grasslands and salt marshes of the Pacific Northwest, where its life history reflects the demands of a relatively short lifespan. In common with many microtine rodents, this species exhibits a maximum recorded longevity of approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years] under field conditions, though few individuals survive beyond their second breeding season due to high predation pressure at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. For a rodent of this size, the basal metabolic rate is notably elevated; respirometry trials conducted at a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] yielded a mean resting oxygen consumption of 85.6 milliliters per hour [JOi = 85.6 milliliters per hour], a value consistent with the energetic demands of high-latitude herbivory. This elevated metabolism is thought to support the rapid tissue production required for early maturation, a strategy that compensates for the high extrinsic mortality typical of tidal marsh environments. The interplay between short lifespan and high metabolic throughput is a defining feature of the life history strategy observed in Microtus townsendii.

Gestation in Townsend's vole is relatively brief, lasting approximately 22 days [tg = approximately 22 days] when measured under common physiological conditions at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], with a reported range of 21 to 23 days that appears consistent across most published accounts. This short gestation period is typical of small-bodied microtines and facilitates the rapid succession of litters during the extended breeding season, which can span from early spring through late autumn in coastal populations. The timing of weaning is similarly compressed; young voles achieve nutritional independence at roughly 13.5 days after birth [tx = roughly 13.5 days after birth] when maternal body temperature is maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a remarkably early age compared to many other rodent species of comparable body mass. Field observations generally report weaning between 13 and 14 days, a narrow window that underscores the precocial nature of the pups' digestive development. This abbreviated dependency period allows females to rapidly resume breeding and maximize their lifetime reproductive output within their constrained lifespan.

Litter size in Microtus townsendii is moderately large, reflecting the species' position along the fast end of the slow-fast life history continuum. Females maintained at a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] typically produce approximately 5 to 6 pups per litter [N_R_i = approximately 5 to 6 pups per litter], with a broader range of 2 to 7 offspring reported in some field studies. When combined with a high frequency of parturition, the reproductive output is substantial; a single female may produce up to 6 litters per year [F_R_i = up to 6 litters per year] during the peak breeding season, yielding an estimated annual production of 30 to 42 pups. This remarkable fecundity is a classic demographic response to the high juvenile mortality characteristic of tidal marsh habitats, where flooding and avian predation impose heavy losses on the pre-weaning cohort. The ability to sustain this elevated reproductive rate depends critically on the female's capacity to maintain a core temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] — a constraint that links thermoregulatory demands directly to population dynamics.

Neonatal body mass in Townsend's vole is modest, with newborn pups weighing approximately 2.8 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.8 grams] at birth, based on measurements taken from captive colonies. The reported range of 2.3 to 3.0 grams is consistent with the altricial condition typical of microtine rodents, where pups are born hairless and with closed eyes, requiring substantial maternal investment during the first week of life. This low birth weight contrasts sharply with the ultimate adult body mass attained by males, which can reach up to 160 grams [Wwi = up to 160 grams] under favorable foraging conditions, with typical values falling between 140 and 160 grams. The roughly 57-fold increase from birth to adult mass necessitates an exceptionally rapid growth trajectory, one that is sustained by the high-quality forage available in coastal wet meadows and by the female's concentrated milk, which is rich in lipids. The magnitude of this postnatal growth is among the highest recorded for arvicoline rodents of similar geographic distribution.

The onset of reproductive maturity in Microtus townsendii occurs relatively early in life, consistent with its overall fast-paced life history. Puberty, defined as the attainment of functional gonadal activity, is typically reached at approximately 290 days after birth [tp = approximately 290 days after birth] when individuals are maintained at a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This relatively late maturation for a small rodent is somewhat surprising given the species' high reproductive output and short lifespan, but it may reflect the energetic constraints imposed by the need to achieve near-adult body size before breeding. Young females that delay reproduction until their first spring following birth are more likely to survive the winter and produce multiple litters in their single breeding season. The onset of puberty appears to be influenced by photoperiod and food availability, but under controlled laboratory conditions, the 290-day estimate has proven remarkably consistent across different study populations. This timing ensures that first litters are born during the period of peak resource abundance in the coastal marsh environment.
